definition.text: A distributed transaction is a transaction that runs across multiple nodes in a network, depending on where the data lives.

facts.text: A distributed transaction must be atomic: it completes in its entirety or not at all, so all nodes commit or all abort and the whole transaction rolls back.
Distributed transactions are not limited to databases, but databases are the common transactional resources, and a transaction often spans a couple of them.
Unlike an ACID transaction on one database, a distributed transaction changes data on several databases, so the system must coordinate commit or rollback of the changes as one self-contained unit.

Isolation is the hard ACID property here: global serializability can be violated even if each database is serializable. Commercial databases that all use strong strict two-phase locking do guarantee global serializability.
Two-phase commit is the common algorithm for completing a distributed transaction correctly, and suits updates that can commit within milliseconds to a couple of minutes.

Long-lived transactions, such as booking a flight, a rental car and a hotel, cannot use two-phase commit because it would lock resources for as long as a day; they use undo steps and compensating transactions instead.
X/Open XA, proposed by The Open Group, became a de facto standard for how the components of a transaction model behave.

definition.text: Two-phase commit is a distributed algorithm that makes all participants in a distributed transaction agree on whether to commit or abort it.

facts.text: One node is the coordinator. In the voting phase it asks all participants to commit; each runs the transaction to the commit point, writes undo and redo log entries, and votes Yes or No.

In the commit phase, if every participant voted Yes, the coordinator sends commit; each participant completes the operation, releases its locks and resources, and acknowledges. The coordinator finishes when all acknowledgements arrive.
If any participant votes No, or the coordinator's timeout expires, the coordinator sends rollback; each participant undoes the transaction from its undo log, releases its locks and acknowledges.

The protocol assumes each node has stable storage with a write-ahead log that survives a crash; participants log protocol states so recovery can finish after a failure. Log records are slow to generate.

Two-phase commit is a blocking protocol: a participant that has voted Yes blocks until it receives commit or rollback, so if the coordinator fails permanently some participants never resolve their transactions.

It cannot dependably recover when the coordinator and a participant both fail during the commit phase: the failed participant may have committed already, so a new coordinator must block until every participant responds.

The protocol works through many temporary failures and is widely used, but it is not resilient to all failure configurations, and in rare cases manual intervention is needed. It is not two-phase locking, a concurrency control protocol.
Two-phase commits are regarded as an anti-pattern in microservices architectures because they tie all participants in the transaction more tightly together.

title: Two-phase commit variants
article: Two-phase commit protocol#Implementing the two-phase commit protocol > Protocol optimizations

definition.text: Two-phase commit variants keep its guarantees while cutting its messages, log writes or completion time.

facts.text: In a common architecture each participant talks only to a nearby transaction manager, and the managers run two-phase commit among themselves; this needs no central component and scales with the number of nodes.

Presumed abort and presumed commit assume a default outcome so that messages and log writes can be skipped; under presumed abort, recovery treats a transaction with no logged commit as aborted. The cost is extra work during failure recovery.
Tree two-phase commit arranges participants as a tree with the coordinator at the root: coordinator messages flow down, and each participant collects the replies from below before passing one up.

Dynamic two-phase commit has no predetermined coordinator: Yes votes race up the tree from the leaves and the node where they meet becomes coordinator, which commits each participant as early as possible.

notes: Also draws on the 'Common architecture' section of the same page.

definition.text: Three-phase commit is a distributed algorithm that makes all nodes agree to commit or abort a transaction, without the indefinite blocking that two-phase commit can suffer.

facts.text: It splits the commit phase of two-phase commit into two: after the vote, the coordinator issues a pre-commit message that every participant must acknowledge, and only then sends the final commit.

The pre-commit state fixes the two-phase commit ambiguity: the coordinator sends doCommit only after all participants have acknowledged they are prepared, so no participant can have committed before all know the decision.
Every phase can time out, so there are no indefinite waits. If the coordinator fails before sending preCommit, the participants agree the operation was aborted.
A recovery coordinator queries the participants: if some are already in the commit phase it drives the protocol to commit; if none received PrepareToCommit it safely aborts.

It assumes bounded network delay and bounded node response times, so with unbounded delays and process pauses it cannot guarantee atomicity, and it needs at least three round trips, which adds latency.
In Skeen's original protocol a quorum can be connected yet unable to make progress; Keidar and Dolev's E3PC refines it so a quorum always can.

title: Saga pattern

definition.text: A saga is a sequence of local transactions that together do the work of one distributed transaction.

facts.text: Each local transaction updates its own database and publishes a message or event that triggers the next local transaction in the saga.
If a local transaction fails, for example by violating a business rule, the saga runs compensating transactions that undo the changes made by the earlier local transactions.
Sagas manage data consistency across services that each own their database, as in microservices, without relying on distributed transactions, which are hard to scale and can hurt performance.

Two ways to coordinate a saga: in choreography each local transaction publishes domain events that trigger local transactions in other services; in orchestration an orchestrator tells the participants which local transactions to run.
Sagas are hard to debug and test, risk cyclic dependencies between participants, and lack of participant data isolation causes durability challenges.
Long-lived transactions hold database resources for a long time, which significantly delays the shorter and more common transactions; sagas were proposed to alleviate this.
The database system guarantees that either every transaction in a saga completes or compensating transactions run to amend a partial execution.

The 1987 paper calls both the concept and its implementation relatively simple, with the potential to improve performance significantly, and also covers running sagas on a system that does not support them directly.

notes: More on an existing entry: new facts from the Sagas paper abstract (García-Molina et al., 1987); no separate paper entry.

definition.text: Heartbeats are periodic signals that let a distributed system monitor the health and status of its components.

facts.text: In push-based heartbeats a node periodically signals another node or a monitoring service, and silence beyond a set interval means failure. It is simple, but network congestion can cause false positives.
In pull-based heartbeats a central monitor periodically asks nodes for status. This reduces network traffic but may make failure detection slower.
A heartbeat can carry health data such as CPU usage, memory usage or application metrics, which allows more nuanced decisions but adds complexity and network overhead.
Timestamps in heartbeats show whether network delays are affecting communication; requiring an acknowledgement shows that the network path between sender and receiver also works.

In consensus systems such as Paxos or Raft, heartbeats help establish or maintain a quorum, a majority of nodes, so enough nodes are operational to decide; this adds complexity when nodes join or leave.

A heartbeat usually goes out at a regular interval of seconds, and if none arrives for a few intervals the sender is assumed to have failed; a short interval costs overhead while a long one makes everything wait.

A false alarm that triggers failover can be highly undesirable, yet real failures need a quick reaction, so the heartbeat transport must be reliable, often over more than one transport such as UDP/IP and a serial link.
The cluster manager keeps a state machine of Down, Init and Alive for each node; an Alive node must acknowledge each periodic heartbeat within a timeout, or it moves to Down.

title: Distributed lock

definition.text: A distributed lock is a mechanism that ensures mutual exclusion across a distributed system.

facts.text: Distributed locks ensure only one node becomes the leader at a time, and that a scheduled task is run by only one worker node, preventing duplicate execution.

They let one process at a time use a shared resource such as a file system, network socket or hardware device, order coordinated updates across microservices and databases, and keep a user session modified by one server.
A distributed lock manager runs on every machine in a cluster with an identical copy of a cluster-wide lock database, so applications on many machines can synchronize access to shared resources.

A resource can be a file, a record or any entity the designer chooses, and resources can form a hierarchy: a parent must be locked before a subordinate. Six lock modes range from null through shared reads to exclusive.

Deadlock arises when processes each hold a lock another needs. The manager periodically checks and returns a deadlock status to one request, and that process must resolve it, for example by releasing its first lock.
The Google SRE book says to use renewable leases with timeouts rather than indefinite locks, because they stop a crashed process holding a lock forever.

Chubby keeps lock information in small files in a replicated database on a Paxos-based fault-tolerant log. ZooKeeper, etcd, Consul and Redis (via the Redlock algorithm) can also provide distributed locks.
Distributed locks are a low-level primitive to use with care; the SRE book says most applications should use a higher-level system that provides distributed transactions.

title: Consensus

definition.text: Consensus is the problem of getting a number of processes, some of which may fail, to agree on a single data value.

facts.text: Consensus protocols must be fault-tolerant: the processes put forward candidate values, communicate with one another, and agree on a single value even though some may fail or be unreliable.
Consensus is used to agree on which transactions to commit to a database and in what order, and underlies state machine replication and atomic broadcast.
One approach is to agree on the majority value, which needs at least one more than half of the votes; but faulty processes may skew the outcome so that consensus is not reached or is reached wrongly.
The output must be the input of some process, since a trivial protocol that always outputs 1 is useless, and a process decides only once, irrevocably.

With halting failures a protocol must give termination (every correct process eventually decides), agreement (all correct processes decide the same value) and validity (if all correct processes propose v, they decide v).
A protocol that guarantees consensus among n processes of which at most t fail is t-resilient; protocols are compared by running time in rounds of message exchange and by message complexity.
Paxos and variants such as Raft are used pervasively in distributed and cloud systems; they depend on an elected leader to make progress and tolerate only crashes, not Byzantine failures.

notes: S:535feb8e8bd4 calls Paxos and Raft 'typically synchronous', which looks wrong next to the FLP section (they stay safe in asynchronous systems); that word was left out.

title: Crash and Byzantine failures
article: Consensus (computer science)#Models of computation > Crash and Byzantine failures

definition.text: A process can fail by crashing, which means it abruptly stops and never resumes, or by a Byzantine failure, where no conditions are imposed on its behavior.

facts.text: A Byzantine process may result from a malicious adversary, may send contradictory or conflicting data to other processes, or may sleep and then resume after a lengthy delay.
Byzantine failures are far more disruptive than crashes, so a protocol that tolerates them must be resilient to every possible error.
Byzantine-tolerant consensus strengthens integrity: if a correct process decides v, then some correct process must have proposed v.
With n processors of which f are Byzantine, no algorithm solves consensus for n ≤ 3f when messages are oral, but protocols exist that tolerate n = f + 1 when messages are written (signed).
Digital signatures give transferable authentication, so each receiver learns who originally created a message, and with them protocols can tolerate a larger number of faults.
Paxos and Raft tolerate only crashes; PBFT is a Byzantine-tolerant protocol listed with the threshold n > 3 f.

title: FLP impossibility result
article: Consensus (computer science)#Models of computation > Asynchronous and synchronous systems > The FLP impossibility result for asynchronous deterministic consensus

definition.text: The FLP result proves that in a fully asynchronous system where even one process may crash, no deterministic algorithm can achieve consensus.

facts.text: Fischer, Lynch and Paterson proved this in 1985: in a fully asynchronous message-passing system with at least one possible crash failure, no deterministic consensus algorithm exists. The result has been mechanically verified, even under fairness assumptions.
FLP does not say consensus can never be reached, only that under the model's assumptions no algorithm can always reach it in bounded time; in practice the bad case is highly unlikely.
Randomized consensus algorithms circumvent FLP by achieving safety and liveness with overwhelming probability, even under worst-case scheduling.

title: Synchronous and asynchronous systems
article: Consensus (computer science)#Models of computation > Asynchronous and synchronous systems

definition.text: In a synchronous system all communication proceeds in rounds, while in an asynchronous system messages have no such round structure.

facts.text: In a synchronous system a process can send all the messages it needs in a round and receive all messages from the others, so no message from one round influences messages sent in the same round.
Real-world communication is often inherently asynchronous, but synchronous systems are easier to model because asynchronous systems naturally involve more issues.
Consensus can be studied in either model; in a fully asynchronous system with a crash failure, the FLP result rules out a deterministic algorithm.

title: Single-value and multi-valued consensus
article: Consensus (computer science)#Models of computation > Inputs and outputs of consensus

definition.text: Single-value consensus agrees on one value, while multi-valued consensus agrees on a series of values over time.

facts.text: In single-value protocols such as Paxos, nodes agree on one value, which can encode metadata such as a transaction committed to a database.
Binary consensus restricts the value to a single binary digit {0,1}; it is not very useful alone but is a building block for general protocols, especially asynchronous ones.

Multi-valued protocols such as Multi-Paxos and Raft agree on a series of values forming a growing history; running single-value consensus repeatedly works, but optimizations and reconfiguration support make dedicated protocols more efficient.

title: Permissioned and permissionless consensus
article: Consensus (computer science)#Models of computation > Permissioned versus permissionless consensus

definition.text: Permissioned consensus runs among a fixed, known group of authenticated participants, while permissionless consensus lets anyone join dynamically.

facts.text: Without a closed group of authenticated members, a Sybil attack can defeat even a Byzantine consensus algorithm by creating enough virtual participants to overwhelm its fault tolerance threshold.

Permissionless protocols counter Sybil attacks with an artificial cost of entry. Bitcoin's proof of work has participants compete to solve hash puzzles, earning the right to commit blocks in proportion to computational effort.
Because proof of work is energy-hungry, later permissionless protocols use proof of stake, proof of space or proof of authority for Sybil protection.

title: Lamport timestamp

definition.text: The Lamport timestamp is a simple logical clock algorithm for ordering events in a distributed system.

facts.text: Clocks on different nodes cannot be perfectly synchronized in practice, so processes use a logical clock: a numeric counter kept in each process that only has meaning relative to the messages moving between processes.

Event A happens-before B if you can get from A to B by moving forward within one process or following a message from send to receive; events in processes that never exchange messages are concurrent and cannot be ordered.

A process increments its counter before each local event and attaches it to every message it sends. On receiving a message it sets its counter to the greater of its own and the message's timestamp, then increments by 1.
The clock guarantees that if a happened-before b then C(a) < C(b), but not the reverse; the two-way strong clock consistency condition needs other techniques such as vector clocks.
A simple Lamport clock gives only a partial ordering; adding an arbitrary tie-breaker such as the process ID makes a total order, but that order is artificial and does not imply causality.
Lamport timestamps say nothing about real time: C(a) < C(b) does not mean a actually happened before b in real time.

Lamport clocks show non-causality but do not capture all causality, which matters when replaying events after a crash: knowing causal relationships lets a node be replayed back to its state while respecting them.
Lamport's 1978 paper examined one event happening before another in a distributed system and showed that this defines a partial ordering of the events.

title: Paxos

definition.text: Paxos is a family of protocols for solving consensus in a network of unreliable or fallible processors.

facts.text: Consensus protocols like Paxos are the basis of state machine replication, and Paxos is usually used where durability is required, such as replicating a file or a database whose durable state may be large.
In most deployments each process plays three roles: Proposer, Acceptor and Learner. Merging the roles collapses the protocol into an efficient client-master-replica style deployment.
Paxos always guarantees safety: only proposed values can be chosen (validity), and no two learners can learn different values (agreement), whatever the pattern of failures.

Paxos is not guaranteed to terminate, consistent with the FLP result that a protocol cannot have safety, liveness and fault tolerance together; the conditions that stall progress are difficult to provoke.
A consensus algorithm can make progress with n = 2F + 1 processors despite F simultaneous failures: the non-faulty processes must outnumber the faulty ones.
Paxos assumes processors of arbitrary speed, asynchronous messages that may take arbitrarily long, and that processors with stable storage may rejoin after a crash.
The Paxos family trades off number of processors, message delays, participant activity, message count and failure types, and can be extended to Byzantine failures such as lying or collusion.
Production systems use it: Google's Chubby lock service, Spanner and Megastore, and DynamoDB for leader election; Cassandra uses it only for lightweight transactions.

notes: Chunk 4 draft: the facts here come from the abstract of 'The part-time parliament' (Lamport, paper>10.1145/279227.279229, primary tier). The chunk 3 draft of this entry holds the protocol. Fold at merge.

definition.text: Basic Paxos is the simplest Paxos protocol: each instance decides a single output value over one or more rounds of two phases.

facts.text: Phase 1a, Prepare: a Proposer sends a Prepare message to at least a Quorum of Acceptors, carrying a unique number n greater than any it used before. n only identifies the message; it is not the proposed value.

Phase 1b, Promise: an Acceptor that sees an n higher than any before replies with a Promise to ignore proposals numbered n or lower, reporting the highest-numbered proposal it has accepted, with its value.
Phase 2a, Accept: once a Quorum has promised, the Proposer sends Accept(n, v). v is the value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal reported, or the Proposer's own value if none was reported.

Phase 2b, Accepted: an Acceptor accepts (n, v) unless it has promised to consider only higher-numbered proposals, then tells the Proposer and Learners; Learners learn the value after Accepted messages from a majority of Acceptors.

Consensus is reached when a majority of Acceptors accept the same identifier number; because each identifier carries one value, they accept the same value, and the chosen value is permanent and immutable.

A round fails when Proposers send conflicting Prepares or no Quorum answers, and a new round starts with a higher number. Losing one Acceptor while a Quorum remains, or a redundant Learner, needs no recovery.
Paxos can elect a leader: a Proposer proposes 'I am the leader', and once a Quorum accepts, every node knows it as the single leader.

title: Multi-Paxos

definition.text: Multi-Paxos runs a continuous series of Basic Paxos instances, with a stable leader, to agree on a stream of commands for a distributed state machine.

facts.text: A typical deployment needs a continuous stream of agreed values acting as commands to a distributed state machine; running a full Basic Paxos for each command would add a significant amount of overhead.
Clients send commands to a leader, which assigns each a new command number i and starts the ith instance of the consensus algorithm with the acceptors.
If the leader is stable, phase 1 (Prepare and Promise) can be skipped for later instances with the same leader, and the round number I travels with each value.
This reduces the failure-free message delay from proposal to learning from 4 delays to 2 delays.
A common deployment collapses Proposer, Acceptor and Learner into one Server role, leaving just Clients and Servers.

notes: Source counts delays two ways: Multi-Paxos 'proposal to learning' (4 down to 2, S:a9d37aae4cda) and Fast Paxos 'client request to learning' (3 for Basic Paxos, S:fcf452f70cca). Both kept as the page states them.

definition.text: Fast Paxos generalizes Basic Paxos to reduce end-to-end message delays.

facts.text: Basic Paxos takes 3 message delays from client request to learning; Fast Paxos allows 2, but needs 3f + 1 acceptors to tolerate f faults (classic: 2f + 1) and the client must send its request to multiple destinations.
When proposals collide, coordinated recovery by the leader with a new round takes four message delays from client to learner.
If the leader specifies a recovery technique in advance, acceptors recover from a collision themselves in three message delays, or two if all Learners are also Acceptors.

definition.text: Cheap Paxos extends Basic Paxos to tolerate F failures with F + 1 main processors and F auxiliary processors, by dynamically reconfiguring after each failure.

facts.text: During stable periods the auxiliary processors take no part in the protocol, so they can be small, slow or cheap processors, or ones mainly devoted to other tasks.
The saving costs liveness: if too many main processors fail in a short time, the system must halt until the auxiliary processors can reconfigure it.
A third processor is needed because with only two, one cannot tell the failure of the other from failure of the communication medium.

title: State machine replication

definition.text: State machine replication is a technique for converting an algorithm into a fault-tolerant, distributed implementation.

facts.text: Consensus protocols are the basis of state machine replication. Ad-hoc techniques may leave important failure cases unresolved, whereas the principled approach proposed by Lamport and others handles all cases safely.
Raft distributes a state machine across a cluster so that each node agrees on the same series of state transitions.
In Raft each client request is a command for the replicated state machines; the leader appends it to its log and applies it to its own state machine once it is committed.
In Paxos deployments, a continuous stream of agreed values acts as commands to a distributed state machine.
The operations of a replicated state machine are ordered globally through a consensus algorithm, which agrees on the sequence while the RSM executes the operations in that order.

Replicated state machines are the building block of data and configuration storage, locking and leader election, and any deterministic program can be made a highly available replicated service by implementing it as one.
Because not every member of the consensus group is in each quorum, an RSM may need to synchronize state from peers, for example with a sliding-window protocol.

notes: No page of its own; mentioned on the Consensus, Paxos and Raft pages.; More on an existing entry: new facts from the Google SRE book chapter 23.

definition.text: Raft is a consensus algorithm designed as an alternative to the Paxos family.

facts.text: Raft was meant to be more understandable than Paxos through separation of logic, yet is formally proven safe. It distributes a state machine across a cluster so every node agrees on the same series of state transitions.

Raft reaches consensus through one elected leader, which alone manages log replication, and decides where new entries go without consulting the other servers. Each server is a leader or a follower, or a candidate during an election.
Raft guarantees election safety (one leader per term), leader append-only, log matching, leader completeness and state machine safety.
Stability needs broadcastTime much less than electionTimeout much less than MTBF, where broadcastTime is the average time to send a request to every server and receive responses.
Membership changes pass through joint consensus, a transitional configuration. Log compaction has each server snapshot its committed entries, and the leader sends snapshots to servers that lag.
In its base form Raft is not Byzantine fault tolerant: nodes trust the elected leader and assume all participants are trustworthy, giving only crash fault tolerance.
The single-leader model sends all reads, writes and log replication through one leader, a single point of failure and a performance bottleneck that does not scale with server workload.
etcd uses Raft to manage a highly-available replicated log, CockroachDB uses it in its replication layer, and MongoDB uses a variant in its replica sets.

title: Raft leader election
article: Raft (algorithm)#Basics > Approach of the consensus problem in Raft > Leader election

definition.text: A Raft leader election starts a new term when the leader fails or the algorithm initializes, and the candidate that wins a majority of votes becomes leader.

facts.text: The leader sends heartbeat messages, and each follower has a timeout, typically 150 to 300 ms, for hearing one. A follower that hears nothing for the election timeout becomes a candidate.

A candidate increases the term counter, votes for itself and requests votes from all other servers. Each server votes once per term, first come first served; a majority of votes makes the candidate leader.
A candidate that sees a larger term number steps down to follower. On a split vote a new term and election start, and a randomized election timeout makes repeated split votes unlikely.

title: Raft log replication
article: Raft (algorithm)#Basics > Approach of the consensus problem in Raft > Log replication

definition.text: In Raft the leader accepts client requests, appends them to its log and replicates them to the followers.

facts.text: The leader forwards each new log entry to followers as AppendEntries messages and retries indefinitely if a follower is unavailable. Once half or more of the followers confirm, the entry is committed and so are all earlier entries.
After a leader crash, logs may be inconsistent; the new leader finds the last entry where a follower's log agrees with its own, deletes the follower's later entries and replaces them with its own.
A candidate cannot win an election unless its log contains all committed entries. Voters compare logs by the term of the last entry, then by length if the terms match.

definition.text: A vector clock is a data structure that determines the partial ordering of events in a distributed system and detects causality violations.

facts.text: A vector clock for n processes is an array of n logical clocks, one per process, and messages carry the sender's clock state as in Lamport timestamps.
Besides its own clock, every process keeps the largest value it has been told of for each other process's clock.

A process increments its own entry on an internal event or a send, and sends a copy of its vector with each message. On receipt it increments its own entry and takes the element-wise maximum with the received vector.
VC(x) is less than VC(y) when every component of VC(x) is at most that of VC(y) and at least one is strictly smaller; if x happened before y, then VC(x) < VC(y).
Lamport's 1978 clocks were scalars and vector clocks generalize them. Vector order implies Lamport order: if VC(a) < VC(b) then C(a) < C(b).

Vector clocks reliably detect causality under crash failures, but under Byzantine failures, where processes behave arbitrarily or maliciously, causality detection is fundamentally impossible for every variant.

Variants cut the space cost. Plausible clocks use less space but may totally order concurrent events; Interval Tree Clocks suit dynamic sets of processes; Bloom clocks use fixed space per node, at the risk of false positives.
Cassandra uses vector clocks to track information currency and ignore outdated state data, and eventual consistency systems use timestamps and vector clocks to detect concurrency between updates.

title: Byzantine fault tolerance

definition.text: A Byzantine fault is a fault that presents different symptoms to different observers, including imperfect information on whether a component has failed; Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT) is resilience to such conditions.

facts.text: In the Byzantine generals allegory the generals must agree on one plan, but traitors may vote selectively, telling some generals to attack and others to retreat, and messengers may fail or forge votes.

A fail-stop failure is only a crash that other nodes detect. A Byzantine failure has no restriction: a node can emit arbitrary data, even looking healthy to some nodes, so it confuses failure detection and is the hardest failure class.
A Byzantine failure need not be a security problem or hostile human interference; it can arise purely from physical or software faults.

Tolerating F Byzantine failures needs at least 3F+1 participants, 2F+1 independent communication paths and F+1 rounds of communication; majority-quorum consensus that tolerates only crashes needs just 2f+1 replicas for f failures.

With unforgeable digital signatures, BFT is possible with any number of traitors provided n > F+1; one commander and two lieutenants can then reach consensus despite a single traitor, who cannot impersonate others.

BFT only guarantees broadcast consistency: every component receives the same value or they agree on a common one. It does not check the value, so a component that consistently sends the same wrong value is not caught.

Blockchains use BFT-based consensus such as PBFT, Tendermint and Avalanche, which tolerate up to one-third faulty or malicious nodes; Bitcoin's proof of work also overcomes Byzantine failures to reach a coherent global view.
Real-time systems such as Boeing 777 flight control use BFT and need very low latency; the SAFEbus network achieves Byzantine fault tolerance within about a microsecond of added latency.

notes: Extends the existing Crash and Byzantine failures entry with the Byzantine fault page; the history, military and AI sections were skipped as trivia.

definition.text: A compensating transaction is a transaction that reverses the effects of a previously committed transaction.

facts.text: It is needed when a business process of several transactions fails after some steps have already committed. Unlike a rollback, which discards uncommitted changes, it is a new transaction that applies business logic to semantically undo completed work.

A compensating transaction is the logical inverse of the original, such as crediting $100 to undo a debit of $100. Each step needs its own, and on failure the compensations of completed steps run in reverse order.
It is fundamental to the saga pattern: each service commits locally with a compensation ready, which avoids holding locks for long periods as distributed two-phase commit does.

Limits: the original results are visible before they are compensated, a compensation can itself fail and needs retries or manual intervention, and some effects cannot be undone, such as a sent email, so the state is only semantically consistent.

title: Apache ZooKeeper

definition.text: Apache ZooKeeper is an open-source server for highly reliable distributed coordination of cloud applications.

facts.text: It offers a hierarchical key-value store that serves as a distributed configuration service, synchronization service and naming registry for large distributed systems.
Data lives in a hierarchical name space like a file system or tree; clients read and write the nodes and so share configuration.

The service is replicated over an ensemble of servers, each holding the whole data tree in memory plus a transaction log and snapshots on disk. Clients keep a TCP connection for requests, heartbeats and watch events.
ZooKeeper can be viewed as an atomic broadcast system in which updates are totally ordered; the ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast (ZAB) protocol is the core of the system.
Typical uses are naming, configuration management, data synchronization, leader election, message queues and notification; it can also implement barriers and distributed locks.
It is fast for read-dominant workloads, scales by adding nodes, and was modeled after Google's Chubby lock service.

The Google SRE book says ZooKeeper was the first open-source consensus system to gain traction because it was easy to use, even for applications not designed for consensus; many applications use consensus as clients of such a service.

notes: Product entry: interviews name ZooKeeper as a coordination building block. One fact cites the SRE book chapter 23.

title: Happened-before relation

definition.text: The happened-before relation orders events by their potential causal relationship in a concurrent system, especially an asynchronous distributed system.

facts.text: It is the least strict partial order in which events in one process follow their occurrence order and a message send precedes its receive; it is transitive, irreflexive and asymmetric.
Events in processes that exchange no messages, directly or through third parties, are concurrent: neither a happened before b nor b before a.
Processes cannot know the relation unless they use a logical clock such as a Lamport clock or vector clock; it supports mutual exclusion algorithms and debugging or optimizing distributed systems.
Under crash failures it can be tracked accurately with vector clocks, but under Byzantine faults it is impossible to detect, because Byzantine processes can forge or manipulate the metadata.

notes: Lamport timestamp and Vector clock entries already carry the happened-before definition in a fact; this entry holds the formal relation.

definition.text: Atomic broadcast, or total order broadcast, is a broadcast in which all correct processes receive the same set of messages in the same order.

facts.text: It is called atomic because it either completes correctly at all participants or all abort without side effects, and it is an important distributed computing primitive.
It is usually required to give validity, uniform agreement, uniform integrity (each message received at most once, and only if broadcast) and uniform total order.
Total order is not FIFO order or causal order; it only requires every participant to receive messages in the same order, with no constraint tied to the order of sending.
Without failures it is easy: all participants follow a leader that decides the order. It is hard when computers fail, for example when the leader fails at the wrong time.

With crash failures atomic broadcast and consensus are equivalent. Consensus reduces to it by proposing a value as a broadcast and deciding the first message received; the reverse runs consensus repeatedly on the next message.
The FLP result therefore applies to atomic broadcast too; it can still be implemented in practice by assuming less than FLP does, for example about processor and communication timings.

Chandra-Toueg is a consensus-based algorithm, and ZAB underpins ZooKeeper. State machine replication assumes atomic broadcast of every event, and atomic broadcast algorithms introduce head-of-line blocking while removing a centralized server's single point of failure.

definition.text: The Two Generals' Problem is a thought experiment that illustrates the pitfalls of coordinating an action over an unreliable communication link.

facts.text: Two generals can only communicate by messengers sent through enemy territory, where any messenger may be captured, yet their armies must attack at the same time or the lone attacker dies.
An acknowledgement can be lost as easily as the original message, so no number of confirmations leaves each general sure the other agreed; a potentially infinite series of messages would be needed.

It was the first computer communication problem proven unsolvable: for any deterministic protocol, the sender of the last delivered message cannot tell whether it arrived, which yields a contradiction.

Because it is unsolvable, generalizations such as the Byzantine Generals problem are unsolvable under arbitrary communication failures, and TCP cannot guarantee state consistency between its endpoints.
In practice engineers accept the uncertainty and reduce it to an acceptable degree, for example by sending many messengers; no rule can be certain to prevent one general attacking without the other.

definition.text: Distributed consensus algorithms only let nodes agree on a value once, so they are used inside higher-level components such as datastores, configuration stores, queues, locks and leader election services.

facts.text: Using higher-level components reduces complexity for designers and lets the underlying consensus algorithm change. Many systems use consensus as clients of a service such as ZooKeeper, Consul, etcd or Google's Chubby.

Replicated datastores apply replicated state machines and put consensus in the critical path, so performance, throughput and scale matter, and the read consistency semantics offered greatly affect scaling.

A single leader gives coarse-grained mutual exclusion. A service written as a simple program can be made highly available by replicating it and electing one leader; consensus is then off the critical path, so throughput matters less.

A barrier blocks a group of processes until a condition is met, splitting a computation into phases, as when MapReduce waits for its whole Map phase. A lone coordinator is a single point of failure; use a replicated state machine.

Distributed queues should use leases rather than outright removal so claimed tasks are processed. Losing the queue stops the whole system, so implementing it as a replicated state machine makes it more robust.

Queues and publish-subscribe systems often need good throughput but not very low latency; atomic broadcast, where all participants receive messages reliably in the same order, is a powerful primitive for them.

title: Consensus performance

definition.text: Consensus is often thought too slow for high throughput and low latency, but the SRE book says this is untrue: implementations can be slow, yet a number of techniques improve performance.

facts.text: No algorithm is best: performance depends on the workload (peak proposals per unit of time, share of writes, read consistency required, request size) and on deployment (local or wide area, quorum placement, sharding, pipelining, batching).

Two physical limits are network round-trip time and persistent-storage write time. Round trips take about a millisecond within a datacenter, a typical 45 milliseconds within the United States and 70 from New York to London.

Stable-leader protocols such as Multi-Paxos, Zab and Raft need one round trip to a quorum, but every write goes through the leader: distant clients pay latency, its outgoing bandwidth is a bottleneck, and a slow leader slows everything.

Fast Paxos lets clients send proposals straight to the acceptors, but it is not always faster: with a slow client link and fast links among acceptors, classic Paxos wins, and client proposers make batching harder.

Batching several client operations into one proposal amortizes the fixed costs of disk logging and network latency. Pipelining keeps several proposals in flight, usually together with batching, without breaking global ordering.

Acceptors must log commitments to disk so a restarted node honors them. A write takes one to several milliseconds; if a small random write takes about 10 milliseconds, consensus is limited to roughly 100 operations per second.

Reads can go to any replica when stale data only causes extra work. A strongly consistent read needs a read-only consensus operation, a stable leader, or quorum leases: brief read leases held by a quorum, at some cost to writes.

With very many clients, regional proxies can hold persistent TCP connections to the consensus group, avoiding connection setup over long distances, and can also encapsulate sharding, load balancing and discovery of members and leaders.

notes: From Google SRE book chapter 23; the SRE book's own figures are cited as given.

title: Sizing a consensus group

definition.text: Consensus systems use majority quorums, so a group of 2f + 1 replicas tolerates f failures, and the number of replicas is one of the most critical deployment decisions.

facts.text: Without Byzantine tolerance the minimum is three replicas, which tolerate one failure; with two, no failure can be tolerated. Byzantine tolerance needs 3f + 1 replicas for f failures.

Most downtime is planned maintenance, which three replicas survive, but an unplanned failure during maintenance makes the group unavailable. Five replicas are therefore recommended, tolerating two failures.

A typical ZooKeeper or Chubby deployment uses five replicas, needs three for quorum and survives two (40%) down. With six, four are needed and only 33% can be down, so adding a replica can reduce availability.

If too many replicas are lost to form a quorum, the group is in theory unrecoverable, because a missing replica's durable log may hold a decision. Forcing a membership change risks data loss; recovered replicas must catch up.
A slow minority of replicas can lag while the quorum of faster ones runs quickly; if replica speeds vary a lot, each failure may force slow outliers into the quorum and lower performance.

Each replica costs resources, and in a sharded system where every shard is a full consensus group the cost grows with the shard count. The number of replicas trades off reliability, frequency of planned maintenance and performance.
Sharded deployments add capacity by adding shards, while read capacity can grow by adding replicas when reads may go to non-leaders; a strong leader takes more load from extra replicas.

notes: Practice advice from Google SRE book chapter 23; the numbers are the book's.

title: Placing consensus replicas

definition.text: Where to put the processes of a consensus cluster trades off the failure domains the system should survive against its latency requirements.

facts.text: A failure domain is the set of components one failure can make unavailable, such as a machine, a rack, a datacenter or a region. As replicas move farther apart they survive bigger failures but round-trip time and operation latency rise.

Widening the failure domain is not always worthwhile: if all clients sit in one domain, spreading further adds cost and latency for no benefit. Snapshots still need backing up elsewhere, and software bugs and human error remain failure domains.
Client-perceived latency is the key measure, so place replicas to minimize client round-trip time. Over a wide area, leaderless protocols such as Mencius or Egalitarian Paxos may have an edge.
Colocating replicas can hurt availability: with five datacenters and a sixth replica added in one of them, an outage there removes both spare replicas and cuts capacity by 33%.

A simple majority quorum is weak when replica round-trip times differ greatly: across the US and Europe, losing the east coast linchpin replica raises latency sharply. A hierarchical quorum of nine replicas in three groups of three helps.

Leaders send full proposals while replicas send small acknowledgements, so leaders use more outgoing bandwidth; in highly sharded systems leaders should be spread across datacenters, since colocated leaders failing over together shift traffic abruptly.
Sending every read to the nearest replica can cascade: a load spike, often from batch jobs starting together, overwhelms the nearest replica, then the next closest, and so on.

notes: Practice advice from Google SRE book chapter 23 (Location of Replicas and Capacity and Load Balancing).

definition.text: Consensus systems are monitored for the number and health of group members, whether a leader exists, how often leadership changes and whether the system makes progress.

facts.text: Track how many members run in each group and each one's status: a process may run yet be unable to progress, may lag persistently, may be recovering state from peers, may be up to date, or may be the leader.
A leader-based system such as Multi-Paxos with no leader is totally unavailable, so the existence of a leader must be monitored.
Rapid leadership changes hurt performance. A term or view number marks each change: a fast increase signals a flapping leader, perhaps from network problems, and a decrease signals a serious bug.

The consensus transaction number should keep rising in a healthy system. Also watch proposals seen against proposals agreed, latency distributions for proposal acceptance, and the time acceptors spend on durable logging.
